# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: Clinical Evidence, Technological Evolution, and Future Horizons

## Pathophysiological Rationale
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a primary driver of cardioembolic stroke [1]. In non-valvular AF, pathophysiological evidence confirms that more than 90% of stroke-inducing thrombi originate within the highly trabeculated left atrial appendage (LAA) [2]. While long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC)—traditionally with vitamin K antagonists and more recently with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs)—remains the standard of care for stroke prophylaxis, it is significantly limited in clinical practice [3]. Many patients experience poor compliance, high bleeding rates, or have relative or absolute contraindications to long-term pharmacotherapy [3]. Consequently, transcatheter percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as a crucial mechanical alternative for stroke prevention [3].

## Clinical Evidence and Landmark Trials
The clinical foundation for LAAC was established by the PROTECT AF [4] and PREVAIL [5] randomized controlled trials, which compared the first-generation Watchman device against warfarin [4, 5]. A patient-level meta-analysis of their 5-year follow-up data demonstrated that mechanical closure offers comparable ischemic stroke protection while significantly reducing hemorrhagic stroke, non-procedural bleeding, and all-cause mortality compared to warfarin [6]. Real-world registries, such as EWOLUTION [7], confirmed the safety and efficacy of the device in routine clinical practice, particularly in patients contraindicated for long-term OAC, a high-risk cohort previously evaluated in the non-randomized ASAP registry [8].

Over the past decade, substantial hardware refinements have aimed to optimize sealing and reduce procedural complications. The next-generation Watchman FLX device, evaluated in the PINNACLE FLX trial [9], introduced a redesigned distal end to prevent thromboembolic events and simplify repositioning. Concurrently, the dual-seal Amplatzer Cardiac Plug [10] and its successor, the Amplatzer Amulet [11], have offered a plug-and-disc design that achieves high complete occlusion rates. The global Amulet registry confirmed the favorable performance of this design in real-world cohorts [12]. Furthermore, specialized devices like the LAmbre have expanded the anatomical feasibility of LAAC to patients with highly complex or exceptionally large appendages [13]. Head-to-head comparisons, such as the SWISS-APERO trial, have underscored that while contemporary devices exhibit comparable clinical endpoints, subtle differences in deployment success and residual leak profiles exist [14].

An important milestone was the PRAGUE-17 trial, which directly compared LAAC (using Watchman or Amulet devices) with DOACs in a high-risk cohort [15]. Its 4-year outcomes demonstrated that LAAC is non-inferior to DOACs for a composite of cardioembolic events and clinically significant bleeding [16]. More recently, the landmark OPTION trial established that LAAC is non-inferior to standard OAC and significantly reduces non-procedure-related bleeding in patients who have undergone catheter ablation for AF [17]. These findings are complemented by surgical data, such as the LAAOS III trial, which showed that concomitant surgical LAA occlusion during cardiac surgery significantly reduces the long-term risk of stroke [18].

## Expert Consensus and Patient Selection
Reflecting this expanding body of evidence, professional societies have formalized the role of percutaneous closure. Expert consensus from the European Heart Rhythm Association (EHRA) and the European Association of Percutaneous Cardiovascular Interventions (EAPCI) [19], along with guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [20] and the joint American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA/HRS) task force [21], recommend LAAC for patients with non-valvular AF who have a clear contraindication to long-term oral anticoagulation.

To ensure successful implantation, meticulous pre-procedural planning is mandatory. Consensus recommendations advocate for cardiac computed tomography (CT) as a high-resolution tool for precise three-dimensional sizing and anatomical evaluation [22]. Real-world registry data from the National Cardiovascular Data Registry (NCDR) highlight that pre-procedural CT or magnetic resonance imaging planning is associated with higher implantation success and fewer resized devices [23]. Intraprocedurally, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remains the historical standard. However, intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) has emerged as a robust alternative. As demonstrated in a large-scale SURPASS post-approval analysis, ICE-guided LAAC achieves comparable safety and efficacy to TEE while avoiding general anesthesia and esophageal trauma [24].

## Complications and Future Directions
Despite the high success rate of modern procedures, long-term monitoring is vital to address device-related thrombus (DRT) and peridevice leak (PDL). An analysis of landmark clinical trials showed that DRT occurs in approximately 3.7% of patients and is associated with a significantly elevated risk of ischemic stroke [25]. Registry data suggest that individual patient characteristics and procedural factors, rather than the type of post-procedural antithrombotic regimen, drive DRT formation [26]. Furthermore, PDL remains a critical clinical concern; even small residual leaks (>2 mm and especially >5 mm) have been shown to predict long-term thromboembolic events at 5-year follow-up [27], a finding corroborated by large-scale real-world registries [28].

The clinical landscape continues to evolve. While LAAC has historically been reserved as a second-line therapy for patients with contraindications to oral anticoagulants, two massive ongoing trials aim to challenge this boundary. The CHAMPION-AF trial [29] (evaluating the Watchman FLX) and the CATALYST trial [30] (evaluating the Amplatzer Amulet) are designed to compare LAAC directly with DOACs as a first-line therapy. The results of these trials are expected to redefine the treatment paradigm, potentially positioning percutaneous LAA closure as a primary, first-line option for stroke prevention in a much broader population of patients with atrial fibrillation.
